title: Records: value semantics and their traps
description: What a record generates and where it bites: normalization in the compact constructor, defensive copies, BigDecimal scale and double comparison in equals, records as composite keys, and a toString that prints every component (JDK 17).

exercises.title: Normalize a record in its constructor, not its accessor
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Our `Email` record lower-cases in its accessor, yet a `HashSet<Email>` still holds `Ana@X.io` and `ana@x.io` as two users. Why, and where does the normalization belong?"

**Why it matters.** A record's generated `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString` read the component FIELDS, not the accessor methods. Overriding `value()` to return a cleaned string changes what callers see but not what equality compares. The one place that can change the stored value is the canonical constructor; in its compact form you reassign the parameter and the field is assigned from it afterwards.

**Your task.** Write the compact constructor of `record Email(String value)`:
- `null` is refused with `IllegalArgumentException("invalid email")`
- trim surrounding whitespace and lower-case with `Locale.ROOT`
- after that the value must contain exactly one `@` with at least one character on each side, else `IllegalArgumentException("invalid email")`
- store the cleaned value, so `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString` all see it

**Worked example.** `new Email("  Ana@X.io ")` equals `new Email("ana@x.io")` and prints `Email[value=ana@x.io]`.
hints: Equality on a record looks at what is stored, so the stored value itself has to be the clean one.
Do the cleaning in the compact constructor by reassigning the parameter, then check the shape of the cleaned value: one at sign, with text before it and after it.
Refuse null first, strip and lower-case with the root locale, find the first and last at sign and require them to be the same position strictly inside the string.

exercises.title: A record that owns its list
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "`Order` is a record, so it is immutable, right? Then why did an order's lines change after we saved it?"

**Why it matters.** A record's fields are final, but a final field that holds an `ArrayList` still points at a list anyone can change: the caller who passed it in, or a caller who got it from the accessor. `Collections.unmodifiableList(list)` only wraps the caller's list, so changes to the original still show through. `List.copyOf` makes an independent, unmodifiable copy (and refuses `null` elements).

**Your task.** Complete `record Order(String id, List<String> lines)`:
- the compact constructor stores an independent, unmodifiable copy of `lines`; a `null` line is refused with `NullPointerException`; an empty list is allowed
- `Order withLine(String line)` returns a NEW order with `line` appended; the original is unchanged
- because the stored list is a `List`, an order built from an `ArrayList` equals one built from `List.of` with the same lines

**Worked example.** `var src = new ArrayList<>(List.of("tea")); var o = new Order("o-1", src); src.add("cake");` leaves `o.lines()` as `[tea]`.
hints: Final only freezes the reference. Ask who else holds a reference to the same list after construction.
Take a copy in the compact constructor that nobody else can reach and nobody can modify, and make the wither build a fresh list for the new order.
Reassign the list parameter to an unmodifiable copy in the compact constructor, and in the wither copy the lines into a new list, append, and construct a new order from it.

exercises.title: A money record that 1.5 and 1.50 agree on
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Two refunds of EUR 1.50 do not match in our reconciliation: one arrived as `1.5`. Both are `Money` records. Fix the type, not the reconciliation."

**Why it matters.** A record compares a `BigDecimal` component with `BigDecimal.equals`, which compares the unscaled value AND the scale: `1.5` and `1.50` are not equal and have different hash codes. Fixing the scale in the constructor makes equality, hashing and printing agree. `stripTrailingZeros` is the wrong fix: `10.00` becomes `1E+1`.

**Your task.** Complete `record Money(BigDecimal amount, String currency)`:
- the compact constructor stores `amount` with scale 2; an amount with more than 2 non-zero decimals (`1.505`) is refused with `ArithmeticException` (do not round money silently); `1.500` is fine
- `currency` must be three letters; store it upper-case (`Locale.ROOT`), else `IllegalArgumentException("bad currency")`
- `Money plus(Money other)` adds amounts of the same currency; another currency is refused with `IllegalArgumentException("currency mismatch")`

**Worked example.** `new Money(new BigDecimal("1.5"), "eur")` equals `new Money(new BigDecimal("1.50"), "EUR")` and prints `Money[amount=1.50, currency=EUR]`.
hints: The record compares the stored amount as BigDecimal does, and BigDecimal counts digits after the point as part of the value.
Give every amount the same scale when the record is built, choosing the rounding mode that refuses to change the value, and clean up the currency in the same place.
Reassign the amount to its scale-two form with the mode that throws when rounding is needed, check the currency is three letters and store it upper-case, and add only matching currencies.

exercises.title: Write the equals a record would write for doubles
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "We are converting `record Reading(String sensor, double value)` into a class (a framework needs a no-arg constructor). Keep its equality exactly as the record had it."

**Why it matters.** A record compares a `double` component as `Double.compare` does, not with `==`: two `NaN` readings are EQUAL (with `==` NaN is never equal to anything, so a set of readings would grow forever), while `0.0` and `-0.0` are NOT equal (with `==` they are). `hashCode` must agree, which `Double.hashCode` does.

**Your task.** Complete the final class `ReadingClass` (fields `sensor` and `value` are given) so that for any two instances `equals` gives the same answer as the given `record Reading`, and `hashCode` keeps the contract:
- `equals`: same class, `Objects.equals` on `sensor`, `Double.compare(value, other.value) == 0`
- `hashCode`: combine `sensor` and `value` so that equal objects have equal hash codes (`Objects.hash(sensor, value)` does; the record's own formula is unspecified, so only the contract is checked)
- `equals(null)` and an object of another class are `false`

**Worked example.** `new ReadingClass("t1", Double.NaN).equals(new ReadingClass("t1", Double.NaN))` is `true`, like the record; `new ReadingClass("t1", 0.0).equals(new ReadingClass("t1", -0.0))` is `false`, like the record.
hints: Two comparisons of doubles disagree on exactly two kinds of value. Find out which one the record uses.
Compare the sensors with a null-safe equality and the values with the comparison method of the Double class, and build the hash from both fields the same way the record does.
Return true for the same object, false for null or another class, then compare sensors null-safely and values with the double comparison method equal to zero, and hash both fields together.

exercises.title: Group by a record key, not a glued string
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "The daily revenue report shows customer `ab` on day `c` with revenue that belongs to customer `a` on day `bc`. The grouping key is `customer + day`."

**Why it matters.** Gluing fields into one string key collides whenever one field can end where another begins (`"ab" + "c"` and `"a" + "bc"`), and a separator only moves the problem to values that contain the separator. A small record is an exact composite key: its `equals` and `hashCode` compare the fields one by one.

**Your task.** Implement `static Map<DayKey, Long> revenueByCustomerAndDay(List<Sale> sales)` with `record DayKey(String customer, String day)` as the key:
- sum `cents` per (customer, day)
- return a `TreeMap` ordered by customer, then day (a `Comparator` on the record's accessors)
- an empty list gives an empty map

**Worked example.** Sales `(ab, c, 100)`, `(a, bc, 50)`, `(ab, c, 25)` give `{DayKey[customer=a, day=bc]=50, DayKey[customer=ab, day=c]=125}`.
hints: Any way of joining two strings into one can be produced by two different pairs. Keep the two parts apart.
Use a small record as the key, sum with a map operation that combines a new value with the old one, and give the sorted map a comparator that looks at both parts.
Create a tree map ordered by customer and then by day, and for each sale merge its cents into the entry for a new day key, summing with the old total.

exercises.title: The record whose toString printed the password
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "A login failure log line contains `Credentials[user=ana, password=hunter2]`. Nobody wrote that toString."

**Why it matters.** A record generates `toString` from every component, so a record holding a secret prints it wherever it is logged, including inside another record, whose `toString` calls the components' own `toString`. You may override any of the generated methods; overriding `toString` does not change `equals` or `hashCode`.

**Your task.** Override `toString` in `record Credentials(String user, String password)` so it prints `Credentials[user=<user>, password=***]`:
- the password is always shown as `***`, also when it is `null` or empty
- `equals` and `hashCode` stay the generated ones (they still compare the password)
- a record that contains `Credentials` (the given `LoginAttempt`) prints the masked form with no change of its own

**Worked example.** `new LoginAttempt(new Credentials("ana", "hunter2"), 3).toString()` is `LoginAttempt[credentials=Credentials[user=ana, password=***], attempt=3]`.
hints: The generated text comes from the fields, and an outer record prints its components with their own toString.
Write your own toString for the credentials record only, always printing three stars for the password, and leave the equality methods alone.
Override toString in the credentials record to build the text from the user and a fixed mask, whatever the password holds.
